current.text: Verify that a secrets management solution, such as a key vault, is used to securely create, store, control access to, and destroy backend secrets. These could include passwords, key material, integrations with databases and third-party systems, keys and seeds for time-based tokens, other internal secrets, and API keys. Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts. For an L3 application, this must involve a hardware-backed solution such as an HSM.

master.text: Verify that a secrets management solution, such as a key vault, is used to securely create, store, control access to, and destroy backend secrets. These could include passwords, key material, integrations with databases and third-party systems, keys and seeds for time-based tokens, other internal secrets, and API keys. Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts. For an L3 application, this must involve a hardware-backed solution such as an HSM.

predecessors.text: Verify that a secrets management solution such as a key vault is used to securely create, store, control access to and destroy secrets. ([C8](https://owasp.org/www-project-proactive-controls/#div-numbering))
Verify that consumers of cryptographic services protect key material and other secrets by using key vaults or API based alternatives.

Verify passwords, integrations with databases and third-party systems, seeds and internal secrets, and API keys are managed securely and not included in the source code or stored within source code repositories. Such storage SHOULD resist offline attacks. The use of a secure software key store (L1), hardware TPM, or an HSM (L3) is recommended for password storage.

Verify that cryptographic keys used in verification are stored securely and protected against disclosure, such as using a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) or Hardware Security Module (HSM), or an OS service that can use this secure storage.
Verify that passwords are stored with sufficient protection to prevent offline recovery attacks, including local system access.
Verify that symmetric keys used to verify submitted OTPs are highly protected, such as by using a hardware security module or secure operating system based key storage.

summaries.body:
The 5.0 mapping records V13.3.1 as modified and moved from 4.0.3 V6.4.1, merged from V1.6.2 and V2.10.4, split from V2.9.1, and covering V2.10.3 and V2.8.2. Those predecessors already required a secrets-management solution (key vault) to create, store, control access to, and destroy secrets; consumers of cryptographic services to protect key material via vaults or APIs; passwords, database integrations, seeds, internal secrets, and API keys to be kept out of source and repositories, with TPM/HSM recommended at higher levels; and OTP symmetric keys to be highly protected.

kisasondi updated the V1.6.2 architecture text on 23 February 2019; tghosth marked V6.4.1 against Proactive Control C8 the next day. The current clause consolidates that family into one configuration requirement, adds that secrets must not appear in build artifacts, and states that L3 must use a hardware-backed solution such as an HSM. Git events at the V13.3.1 slot (malicious-code refactor, swapping GraphQL/SOAP per issue 516) are a different chapter occupying the number.

The wording that mattered is the 5.0 consolidation: vault-based secrets management (V6.4.1), architectural key protection (V1.6.2), and the V2.10.4/V2.9.1/V2.8.2 rules about not shipping secrets in source and using TPM/HSM at higher levels become a single clause that also forbids secrets in build artifacts and makes hardware-backed storage mandatory at L3.

Issue 516 (reorder GraphQL vs SOAP) and vanderaj's 1 January 2019 malicious-code refactor at V13.3.1 are ID-slot reuse, not evolution of this secrets control.
